column2: Weather Station Build Guide
First get to know every component in your kit, understand how a breadboard works, then build a little at a time. Every stage has a small test code, so you know that part works before moving on.
Three rules before you start
Attach or move wires only while the ESP32 is off. Plug the USB back in after everything is checked.
The red line on the breadboard is for voltage (+), the blue line for GND (−). Never connect the two directly.
Compare every wire with the picture and the text in the step. Almost every beginner failure is one wire shifted by one hole.
Get to know your components
All these photos are of your own kit. After reading, turn on guess-the-name mode: each component's name is hidden, try to say it, then tap the card to check.
Basics you need to know
How a breadboard works

Inside the breadboard are metal strips that connect certain holes. Every hole has an address: a row letter (a–j) and a column number (1–30), both printed on your breadboard. So e3 means row e, column 3.
Green: the five holes in one column (a–e) are connected to each other. A component with a leg in a5 is connected to a wire in d5.
Orange: f–j in the same column are also connected, but separated from a–e by the gap in the middle.
Red: the power rail is connected along its whole line. Any hole along the red line is the same.
Different columns are not connected. a5 and a6 are not linked.
The orientation of the breadboard does not matter. What matters is matching the letters and numbers printed on your breadboard.
Three kinds of jumper wire
Male = the end is a metal pin (it can go into a breadboard hole). Female = the end is a hole (it fits over a pin).
Male–male (M-M): breadboard hole to breadboard hole.
Male–female (M-F): expansion board pin to breadboard. The most used in this project.
Female–female (F-F): pin to pin, for example the LCD straight to the expansion board.
Wire color makes no electrical difference. But make a habit of red for +, black or brown for GND, so it is easy to check.
Reading the expansion board
Your ESP32 is plugged into the black expansion board. Every GPIO pin has one row of 3 pins:
S (signal) = the GPIO pin itself, for example D4. The signal wire goes here.
V = the voltage for the component.
The labels on the expansion board use the format D + GPIO number: GPIO 25 = D25. A full explanation of your board is below.
Getting to know your expansion board
This is your own board without the ESP32: the ESP32 ESP32S 30P Expansion board. The numbers in the photo are explained below it.

The voltage selector jumper is labeled 3.3V V 5V. Its black cap connects the middle pin (V) to one of the sides, and that is the voltage of all the V pins on the board. In your photo, the cap appears to be in the V–5V position. For this project move it to the 3.3V–V position: pull the cap straight up (use a fingernail or tweezers), then push it onto the two pins on the 3.3V side.

The right-hand pin rows. Each row has 3 pins. The order is printed underneath: G innermost, V in the middle, S outermost (near the edge of the board). The pin names (D25, D26, D34, ...) are printed beside the S pin. The block labeled GND above them holds extra GND pins.

The left-hand pin rows for D15, D2, D4, D16, D17, D5, D18, D19, D21, RX, TX, D22, D23. The G/V/S order letters under this column cannot be read in your photo. They are usually mirrored (S at the outer edge), but check the letters underneath yourself before attaching wires on this side.
The GND, VCC, D21, D22 header for I2C modules, for example the I2C version of the LCD. Not used yet.
Two long female sockets, where the ESP32 plugs in.
The 6.5–16V DC jack for an adapter. Not used yet; USB power is enough.
The expansion board's micro-USB and USB-C ports, most likely for power only. To upload code, plug the cable into the port on the ESP32 module itself.

The sensors (DHT11, LDR) are given voltage from the red rail, then send a signal to the ESP32 pin at the same voltage. The ESP32 pins are designed for a maximum of 3.3V. Continuously giving them 5V can damage them. If you have a multimeter, after moving the jumper measure the voltage between the V and G pins: the result must be about 3.3V.

Unplug the USB first. Face the ESP32's micro-USB port toward the DC jack and the expansion board's USB port (top), with the ESP32's metal can facing down. Match the D15 label on the ESP32 with the D15 row of the expansion board. Make sure all 30 pins go into the sockets with none left outside, then press down evenly and slowly with both thumbs.
Reading resistor values

The resistors in the kit can have 4 or 5 color bands. Read from the end where the bands are grouped; the last band, set slightly apart, is the tolerance. If your 10 kΩ resistor is brown, black, orange, gold, it has 4 bands and its value is exactly the same as the one below.
The colors on small resistors are sometimes hard to tell apart. A multimeter in Ω mode gives a definite answer. Resistors have no polarity, so they can be fitted either way round.
Build in stages

In every picture, the newly added parts appear bright and the parts from the previous stage appear faded. White dot = a leg or wire end going into a hole. Wires may cross over the breadboard; what matters is that the ends are in the right holes. On a phone, swipe the picture sideways to see the whole breadboard.

If something does not work

The port does not show up in the Arduino IDE: your USB cable may be charge-only, try another cable. If it still does not show up, install the CP210x or CH340 driver (see the text on the small chip near the ESP32's USB port).
Upload stops at "Connecting.....": press and hold the BOOT button on the ESP32 until the upload percentage appears, then release.
The Serial Monitor shows strange letters: change the baud at the bottom right of the Serial Monitor to 115200.
The LED does not light: almost certainly reversed. Unplug the USB, turn the LED around, try again. An LED is not damaged by being reversed.
The ESP32 suddenly switches off or restarts when plugged in: unplug the USB immediately. Usually a wire connects the red rail straight to the blue one (a short circuit).
A part that used to work stops working: wires on the breadboard are often knocked while fitting a new component. Check that stage again with its test code.

The Serial Monitor repeats "load:0xffffffff,len:-1" (keeps restarting): under Tools set Flash Mode to DIO, Flash Frequency to 40MHz, Erase All Flash Before Sketch Upload to Enabled, Upload Speed to 115200, then upload again.

Upload fails halfway after the V/G wires were attached: a wire from the V or G pin may be touching (shorting) or drawing excess current. Unplug all wires from the expansion board, upload first, then reattach the wires one at a time.
The Telegram bot does not reply: make sure the WiFi is 2.4 GHz, the token is correct, the chat ID is correct, and you have pressed Start in the bot.
Still stuck? Photograph your circuit from above in bright light, send it to me, and say which stage.
Full code
Download stasiun_cuaca.ino. Fill in the WiFi name, password, bot token and chat ID at the top of the file before uploading. Do not upload a file that already contains the token to a public place.

This code has been checked to compile successfully with Arduino ESP32 core 3.3.12, with USE_LCD set to both 0 and 1. The LiquidCrystal library is built into the Arduino IDE; if you get the error "LiquidCrystal.h: No such file", install LiquidCrystal by Arduino from the Library Manager.
After the weather station

The sensors, LED and Telegram bot you learn here are used again in the 4WD AI Robot: the DHT11 can become the robot's weather sensor directly, and how to read the Serial Monitor and connect wires on the breadboard is exactly the same.
